aflcio_description: Showing his continuing indifference to the plight of unemployed Americans, President Ford vetoed a $6.1 billion public works jobs bill. This was the third major employment bill approved by the 94th Congress to be erased by a presidential veto. The measure would have created an estimated 600,000 jobs primarily in the construction of much needed public facilities such as schools and libraries and water, sewer and pollution control projects. The House on Feb. 19 successfully overrode the veto by a 319-98 vote. However, the Senate later failed in this effort. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Despite the earlier setback, Congress resurrected and passed a scaled-down version of the vetoed public works measure. The $3.9 billion bill would create over 300,000 jobs. Like the previously vetoed bill, the measure included over $1 billion in aid to financially-strapped cities and states. Again President Ford vetoed the bill. This time, however, Congress rebuffed him. Following the Senate's lead, the House voted 310-96 on July 22 to override the veto. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The House rejected President Ford's veto of a $36 billion appropriations measure for the Departments of Labor and Health, Education & Welfare. The bill significantly increased funds for labor-backed manpower, health, education and job safety programs. The House voted 310-113 on Jan. 27 to override the President's action. The Senate also overrode this veto. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

aflcio_description: President Ford vetoed a stopgap funding bill to help state child care centers comply with federal health and staffing requirements. Financially unable to meet these standards, many of these facilities would be closed down because federal funds would be cut off. Denial of these child care services would force many low-income working mothers back to welfare in order to care for their children. The House on May 4 easily overrode the veto by a 301-101 vote. However, on the following day the Senate sustained the veto. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Another Ford veto blocked legislation giving nearly 2.8 million federal and postal employees the same rights now enjoyed by other Americans to participate in partisan political activities. President Ford based his veto on the erroneous assertion that the bill weakened existing protections against political coercion and intimidation of federal workers when in fact it significantly improved these safeguards. On Apr. 29 the House by a 243-160 margin failed by 25 votes to obtain the two-thirds vote needed to override the veto. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

A priority on labor's legislative agenda, this legislation would provide a mechanism to better coordinate national economic planning and direct it toward the primary economic goal of full employment. Designed to reduce national adult unemployment to a 3 percent rate within four years, the bill sets up a variety of federally-assisted jobs programs to be implemented if other methods of reducing unemployment fail. Start-up planning and administrative funds for the Humphrey-Hawkins bill were provided in the first Congressional Budget Resolution. An effort by Rep. Sarasin (R-Conn.) to strip these funds from the bill was rejected 177-206 on Apr. 29. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Over Administration objections, the House made significant improvements in the nation's housing programs when it passed the 1977 housing authorization bill. Among other provisions, the legislation increased funding available for housing for the elderly and reactivated the public housing construction program. A last-minute motion by Rep. Brown (R-Mich.) to recommit the conference report on the bill to delete these provisions was defeated 157-250 on June 30. For Recommittal - Wrong. Against Recommittal - Right.

On June 24, during debate on a Labor-HEW appropriations bill, the House approved 231-161 an amendment by Rep. Findley (R-Ill.) seriously weakening the 1970 Occupational Safety & Health Act. By excluding firms employing 10 or fewer workers from coverage under the job safety law, this amendment would arbitrarily deny protection to 83 percent of all workplaces and 20 percent of all workers presently covered. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

To prevent jurisdictions utilizing federal revenue-sharing funds from evading the program's minimal Davis-Bacon Act fair wage requirements and thus pay wages lower than those prevailing in the area, the AFL-CIO sought to expand the wage coverage provisions in the revenue-sharing program. Under existing law only projects using 25 percent or more federal funds have to pay the prevailing rate. An amendment by Rep. O'Hara (D-Mich.) to require Davis-Bacon rates whenever any revenue sharing funds are used was defeated 174-218 on June 10. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

House-passed legislation to improve the federal-state system of unemployment compensation benefits fell far short of overall reforms long sought by the AFL-CIO. A key fight on the bill, strongly opposed by business interests, came on an amendment by Rep. Corman (D-Calif.) providing for a uniform federal standard to upgrade the inadequate maximum benefits paid by most states. The labor-backed amendment would have set the benefits at 50 percent of a person's average weekly wage up to a maximum equal to two-thirds of the statewide average weekly wage. The House rejected the amendment by a 113-281 vote on July 20. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Opponents of the unemployment compensation bill sought to eliminate one of the few significant reforms in the legislation. As reported by committee, the bill extended benefit protection to over 8.3 million state and local government workers not previously covered. Rep. Ketchum (R-Calif.) offered an amendment to strike this provision. It was rejected 186-212 on July 20. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

During House debate on legislation reconstructing the Federal Election Commission, conservatives offered a series of amendments to gag labor's political voice. The most serious of these was a proposal by Rep. Wiggins (R-Calif) designed to discourage union political activities by overloading local unions with cumbersome reporting requirements. The Wiggins amendment would have required that all the costs of communicating with members on any election matter would have to be reported. The House rejected the amendment 175-220 on Apr. 1. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

A last minute effort by labor and consumer groups blocked almost certain passage of a proposal to deregulate the price of natural gas sold in interstate commerce. Long sought by the nation's energy interests and solidly backed by the Ford Administration, deregulation would have initially cost American consumers an estimated $5.4 billion yearly, increasing to over $17 billion annually in five to seven years. A compromise amendment by Rep. Smith (D-Iowa) which allowed partial price deregulation for only small gas producers but more importantly extended controls to previously unregulated intrastate gas was approved by a 205-201 vote Feb. 5. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Each year hundreds of miners lose their lives because of lax enforcement of mine safety laws primarily because the Interior Dept. which enforces these laws is also responsible for maximizing mine production. To end this conflict of interest, the AFL-CIO has long proposed the transfer of job safety functions to the Labor Dept. so that all job safety programs might be under one jurisdiction. Legislation to effect this change was passed by the House despite Administration opposition. Rep. Quie (R-Minn.) offered an Administration-backed substitute bill to prevent this transfer. His proposal was rejected by the House on July 27 by a 119-263 vote. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

The nation's federal aid to education program allocates funds to areas "impacted" by federal installations to help defray state and local educational costs of children whose families are employed by these installations. In recent years such "impact" aid was extended to locales having low-rent public housing to help pay the educational cost of children residing in these areas. Long-time antagonists of this program tried to block appropriations for it. During debate on legislation revising educational funding for 1976, Rep. Michel (R-Ill.) offered an amendment to eliminate the $98 million allocated for this educational aid. His amendment was rejected 134-267 on Feb. 10. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

With well over 7 million Americans unemployed, the House approved a two-year expansion of the labor-backed public service jobs program (CETA). The bill would effectively double the number of jobs available to 600,000. Despite increasing unemployment, the Administration sought only an extension of the program at existing levels. A substitute to this effect by Rep. Quie (R-Minn.) was rejected 175-226 Feb. 10. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

During debate on the 1977 Labor-HEW appropriations bill on June 24, the House approved 183-181 an amendment by Rep. Mitchell (D-Md.) increasing funds for the Summer Youth Employment program. This program was created to combat the high rate of unemployment among young workers - more than double that of other age groups. Mitchell's amendment brought funding up to the spending targets set earlier by Congress in the first Budget Resolution. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

The Administration's assault on programs to help the nation's needy continued in 1976. Singled out for special attack was the food stamp program, whose rolls have swelled as a result of soaring unemployment. Regressive Administration guidelines designed to slash millions of working poor and low-income families from the food stamp rolls were blocked by court action, but House conservatives tried to effect these changes through legislative action. During debate on the 1977 agricultural appropriations bill, Rep. Rousselot (R-Calif.) tried to slash over $794 million from the food stamp program. The House rejected his proposal by a 184-222 vote on June 16. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

Blocked in their efforts to deregulate natural gas prices, President Ford and his Federal Energy Administration pushed to end price controls on various oil products. They met with partial success as Congress refused to block a proposal to decontrol prices of diesel fuel, home heating oil and other middle distillate fuels. These fuels supply 17 percent of domestic energy needs. The estimated increased cost on home heating bills alone would be over $1 billion. Although Congress has veto power over such decisions, a resolution to block this proposal was tied up in the House Commerce Committee. A motion by Rep. Dingell (D-Mich.) to discharge the resolution from the committee to allow for its floor consideration was defeated by a 194-208 vote on June 30. As a result, the price decontrol proposal went into effect. For Discharge - Right. Against Discharge - Wrong.

aflcio_description: In 1972 only 55 percent of the electorate voted in the presidential elections. Two years later only 40 percent of eligible voters cast ballots in congressional elections. Millions of American voters fail to go to the polls each year because of state and local registration laws that actually discourage registration to vote. To curb this decline in voter participation, the AFL-CIO endorsed a bill establishing a national postcard voter registration system which the House approved Aug. 9. During debate on the bill, the House defeated 172-199 an amendment by Rep. Frenzel (R-Minn.) to disallow implementation of the postcard system in 1976 elections and thus discourage Senate action this year. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

The AFL-CIO strongly supports federal efforts to develop alternate sources of energy to meet the nation's long-term needs. Nuclear energy is one of these potential sources of power. During debate on legislation providing funds for the Energy Research & Development Administration for 1977, opponents of nuclear energy development again tried to block the continuing construction of the Clinch River breeder reactor demonstration project. An amendment by Rep. Coughlin (R-Pa.) placing severe financing restrictions on the project so as to delay its development was defeated 173-209 on May 20. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

The AFL-CIO has urged termination of U.S. contributions to the United Nations Development Program (UNDP). This UN agency, which is charged with promoting economic growth and stability in under-developed nations, has squandered millions in funding and mismanaged projects which have never been completed. Meanwhile, eastern bloc countries and oil-rich Arab states have received funds far in excess of their contributions to the UNDP. During House debate on foreign aid appropriations for 1977, Rep. Edwards (R-Ala.) introduced an amendment to delete $85.5 million allocated to the UNDP. The House rejected his proposal 179-208 on Mar. 4. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

During House debate on a 1977 defense authorization bill, numerous attempts were made to block or delay development of various weapons systems. One such amendment offered by Rep. Seiberling (D-Ohio) would have deferred the expenditure of $960 million for the development of the B-1 strategic bomber until after Feb. 1977. The House rejected the amendment 177-210 on Apr. 8. For - Wrong. Against - Right.
